In [[mathematics]] and [[electronics]], '''cavity perturbation theory''' describes methods for derivation of [[perturbation theory|perturbation]] [[formula]]e for performance changes of a [[Resonator|cavity resonator]].

These performance changes are assumed to be caused by either introduction of a small foreign object into the cavity, or a small deformation of its boundary. Various mathematical methods can be used to study the characteristics of cavities, which are important in the field of microwave systems, and more generally in the field of electro magnetism.

There are many industrial applications for cavity resonators, including microwave ovens, microwave communication systems, and remote imaging systems using electromagnetic waves. How a resonant cavity performs can affect the amount of energy that is required to make it resonate, or the relative stability or instability of the system.

==Introduction==

When a resonant cavity is perturbed, e.g. by introducing a foreign object with distinct material properties into the cavity or when the shape of the cavity is changed slightly, [[electromagnetic fields]] inside the cavity change accordingly. This means that all the resonant modes (i.e. the [[quasinormal mode]]) of the unperturbed cavity slightly change. 
Analytically predicting how the perturbation changes the optical response is a classical problem in electromagnetics, with important implications spanning from the radio-frequency domain to present-day nano-optics. The underlying assumption of cavity perturbation theory is that electromagnetic fields inside the cavity after the change differ by a very small amount from the fields before the change. Then [[Maxwell's equations]] for original and perturbed cavities can be used to derive analytical expressions for the resulting resonant frequency shift and linewidth change (or [[Q factor]] change) by referring only to the original unperturbed mode (not the perturbed one).

==General theory==

It is convenient to denote cavity frequencies with a complex number <math>\tilde\omega=\omega-i\gamma/2</math>, where  <math>\omega=Re(\tilde\omega)</math> is the [[angular resonant frequency]] and <math>\gamma=2Im(\tilde\omega)</math> is the inverse of the mode lifetime. Cavity perturbation theory has been initially proposed by Bethe-Schwinger in optics <ref>{{Cite journal|title = Perturbation theory for cavities |journal = N.D.R.C. RPT. D1-117 Cornell University |volume = 12 |article-number = 1700113 |year = 2018|first1 = H. A.  |last1 = Bethe |first2 = J. |last2 = Schwinger|issue = 5 |doi = 10.1002/lpor.201700113|arxiv = 1705.02433|bibcode = 2018LPRv...1200113L |s2cid = 51695476 }}</ref>
, and Waldron in the [[radio frequency]] domain.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Perturbation theory of resonant cavities |url = https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/5245404|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200218213325/https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/5245404|archive-date = February 18, 2020|journal = Proc. Inst. Electr. Eng.  |date = September 1960|pages = 272–274|volume = 107 |issue = C |doi = 10.1049/pi-c.1960.0041|first = R. A.  |last = Waldron|url-access = subscription}}</ref> These initial approaches rely on formulae that consider stored energy 
{{NumBlk|:|<math>\frac{\tilde\omega - \tilde\omega_0}{\tilde\omega_0}\thickapprox -\frac{\iiint_{V}\Delta\epsilon |E_0|^2 dv}{\iiint_{V}(\mu_0 |H_0|^2+\epsilon |E_0|^2)dv}\,</math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}
where <math>\tilde\omega</math> and <math>\tilde\omega_0</math> are the complex frequencies of the perturbed and unperturbed cavity modes, and <math>H_0</math> and <math>E_0</math> are the electromagnetic fields of the unperturbed mode (permeability change is not considered for simplicity). Expression ({{EquationNote|1}}) relies on stored energy considerations. The latter are intuitive since common sense dictates that the maximum change in resonant frequency occurs when the perturbation is placed at the intensity maximum of the cavity mode. However energy consideration in electromagnetism is only valid for Hermitian systems for which energy is conserved. For cavities, energy is conserved only in the limit of very small leakage (infinite Q's), so that Expression ({{EquationNote|1}}) is only valid in this limit. For instance, it is apparent that Expression ({{EquationNote|1}}) predicts a change of the Q factor (<math>Im(\tilde\omega-\tilde\omega_0)</math>) only if <math>\Delta\epsilon</math> is complex, i.e. only if the perturber is absorbent. Clearly this is not the case and it is well known that a dielectric perturbation may either increase or decrease the Q factor.

The problems stems from the fact that a cavity is an open non-Hermitian system with leakage and absorption. The theory of non-Hermitian electromagnetic systems abandons energy, i.e. <math>|E.E|</math> products, and rather focuses on <math>E.E</math> products <ref>{{Cite journal|title = Light interaction with photonic and plasmonic resonances|journal = Laser & Photonics Reviews|date = 2018-04-17|article-number = 1700113|volume = 12|issue = 5|doi = 10.1002/lpor.201700113|first1 = P. |last1 = Lalanne|first2 = W. |last2 = Yan |first3 = K. |last3 = Vynck |first4 = C. |last4 = Sauvan |first5 = J.-P. |last5 = Hugonin|arxiv = 1705.02433|bibcode = 2018LPRv...1200113L|s2cid = 51695476}}</ref> that are complex quantities, the imaginary part being related to the leakage. To emphasize the difference between the normal modes of Hermitian systems and the resonance modes of leaky systems, the resonance modes are often referred to as [[quasinormal mode]]. In this framework, the frequency shift and the Q change are predicted by
{{NumBlk|:|<math>\frac{\tilde\omega - \tilde\omega_0}{\tilde\omega_0}\thickapprox -\frac{\iiint_{V}\Delta\epsilon E_0^2 dv}{\iiint_{V}(\epsilon E_0^2-\mu_0 H_0^2)dv}\,</math>|{{EquationRef|2}}}}
The accuracy of the seminal equation {{EquationNote|2}} has been verified in a variety of complicated geometries. For low-Q cavities, such as plasmonic nanoresonators that are used for sensing, equation {{EquationNote|2}} has been shown to predict both the shift and the broadening of the resonance with a high accuracy, whereas equation {{EquationNote|1}} is inaccurately predicting both.<ref name="Yang 3439–3444">{{Cite journal|title = Simple Analytical Expression for the Peak-Frequency Shifts of Plasmonic Resonances for Sensing|journal = Nano Letters|date = 2015-04-06|pages = 3439–3444|volume = 15|issue = 5|doi = 10.1021/acs.nanolett.5b00771|pmid = 25844813|first1 = J. |last1 = Yang | first2 = H. |last2 = Giessen | first3 = P. |last3 = Lalanne |arxiv = 1505.04877|bibcode = 2015NanoL..15.3439Y|s2cid = 11999899}}</ref> For high-Q photonic cavities, such as [[photonic crystal]] cavities or microrings, experiments have evidenced that equation {{EquationNote|2}} accurately predicts both the shift and the Q change, whereas equation {{EquationNote|1}} accurately predicts the shift only.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Mapping complex mode volumes with cavity perturbation theory|journal = Optica|date = 2019-03-20|pages = 269–273|volume = 6|issue = 3|doi = 10.1364/OPTICA.6.000269|first = K.C. |last = Cognée|arxiv = 1811.11726|bibcode = 2019Optic...6..269C|s2cid = 119439374}}</ref>

The following sections are written with <math>|E.E|</math> products; however, they should be understood with the <math>E.E</math> products of quasinormal mode theory.

==Material perturbation==

[[File:Electromagnetic cavity perturbation.svg|thumb|center|upright=3|Cavity material perturbation]]

When a material within a cavity is changed ([[permittivity]] and/or [[Permeability (electromagnetism)|permeability]]), a corresponding change in resonant frequency can be approximated as:<ref name=Pozar1998>[[David M. Pozar|David Pozar]], Microwave Engineering, 2nd edition, Wiley, New York, NY, 1998.</ref>

{{NumBlk|:|<math>\frac{\omega - \omega_0}{\omega_0}\thickapprox -\frac{\iiint_{V}(\Delta\mu |H_0|^2+\Delta\epsilon |E_0|^2)dv}{\iiint_{V}(\mu |H_0|^2+\epsilon |E_0|^2)dv}\,</math>|{{EquationRef|3}}}}

where <math>\omega</math> is the [[angular frequency|angular]] [[resonant frequency]] of the perturbed cavity, <math>\omega_0</math> is the resonant frequency of the original cavity, <math>E_0</math> and <math>H_0</math> represent original [[electric field|electric]] and [[magnetic field]] respectively, <math>\mu</math> and <math>\epsilon</math> are original [[Permeability (electromagnetism)|permeability]] and [[permittivity]] respectively, while <math>\Delta\mu</math> and <math>\Delta\epsilon</math> are changes in original permeability and permittivity introduced by material change.

Expression ({{EquationNote|3}}) can be rewritten in terms of [[Energy density|stored energies]] as:<ref name=Mathew2005>Mathew, K. T. 2005. Perturbation Theory. Encyclopedia of RF and Microwave Engineering</ref>

{{NumBlk|:|<math>\frac{\omega - \omega_0}{\omega_0}\thickapprox -\frac{1}{W}\iiint_{V}(\frac{\Delta\epsilon}{\epsilon}\cdot\bar{w_e}+\frac{\Delta\mu}{\mu}\cdot\bar{w_m})dv\,</math>|{{EquationRef|4}}}}

where W is the total energy stored in the original cavity and <math>\bar{w_e}</math> and <math>\bar{w_m}</math> are [[Electric potential energy|electric]] and [[Energy density#Energy density of electric and magnetic fields|magnetic energy]] densities respectively.

==Shape perturbation==

[[File:Electromagnetic shape perturbation.svg|thumb|center|upright=3|Cavity shape perturbation]]

When a general shape of a resonant cavity is changed, a corresponding change in resonant frequency can be approximated as:<ref name=Pozar1998 />

{{NumBlk|:|<math>\frac{\omega - \omega_0}{\omega_0}\thickapprox \frac{\iiint_{\Delta V}(\mu |H_0|^2-\epsilon |E_0|^2)dv}{\iiint_{V}(\mu |H_0|^2+\epsilon |E_0|^2)dv}\,</math>|{{EquationRef|5}}}}

Expression ({{EquationNote|5}}) for change in resonant frequency can additionally be written in terms of time-average stored energies as:<ref name=Pozar1998 />

{{NumBlk|:|<math>\frac{\omega - \omega_0}{\omega_0}\thickapprox \frac{\Delta W_m - \Delta W_e}{W_m + W_e}\,</math>|{{EquationRef|6}}}}

where <math>\Delta W_m</math> and <math>\Delta W_e</math> represent time-average [[electric]] and [[magnetic]] energies contained in <math>\Delta V</math>.

This expression can also be written in terms of energy densities <ref name=Mathew2005 /> as:

{{NumBlk|:|<math>\frac{\omega - \omega_0}{\omega_0}\thickapprox \frac{(\bar{w_m}-\bar{w_e})\cdot\Delta V}{W}\,</math>|{{EquationRef|7}}}}

Considerable accuracy improvements of the predictive force of Equation ({{EquationNote|5}}) can be gained by incorporating [[local field]] corrections,<ref name="Yang 3439–3444"/> which simply results from the [[interface conditions for electromagnetic fields]] that are different for the displacement-field and electric-field vectors at the shape boundaries.

==Applications==

Microwave measurement techniques based on cavity perturbation theory are generally used to determine the dielectric and magnetic parameters of materials and various circuit components such as [[dielectric resonator]]s. Since ex-ante knowledge of the resonant frequency, resonant frequency shift and [[electromagnetic field]]s is necessary in order to extrapolate material properties, these measurement techniques generally make use of standard resonant cavities where resonant frequencies and electromagnetic fields are well known. Two examples of such standard resonant cavities are rectangular and circular [[waveguide]] cavities and [[coaxial cable]]s resonators . Cavity perturbation measurement techniques for material characterization are used in many fields ranging from physics and material science to medicine and biology.<ref>{{cite conference | last1=Vyas | first1=A.D. | last2=Rana | first2=V.A. | last3=Gadani | first3=D.H. | last4=Prajapati | first4=A.N. | title=Cavity perturbation technique for complex permittivity measurement of dielectric materials at X-band microwave frequency | publisher=IEEE | year=2008 | isbn=978-1-4244-2690-4 | doi=10.1109/amta.2008.4763128 | pages=836–838|conference=International Conference on Recent Advances in Microwave Theory and Applications}}</ref><ref>[[Wenquan Che]]; Zhanxian Wang; Yumei Chang; Russer, P.; "Permittivity Measurement of Biological Materials with Improved Microwave Cavity Perturbation Technique," Microwave Conference, 2008. EuMC 2008. 38th European, vol., no., pp.905–908, 27–31 Oct. 2008</ref><ref>Qing Wang; Xiaoguang Deng; Min Yang; Yun Fan; Weilian Wang; "Measuring glucose concentration by microwave cavity perturbation and DSP technology," Biomedical Engineering and Informatics (BMEI), 2010 3rd International Conference on, vol.3, no., pp.943–946, 16–18 Oct. 2010</ref><ref>A. Sklyuyev; M. Ciureanu; C. Akyel; P. Ciureanu; D. Menard; A. Yelon; "Measurement of Complex Permeability of Ferromagnetic Nanowires using Cavity Perturbation Techniques," Electrical and Computer Engineering, 2006. CCECE '06. Canadian Conference on, vol., no., pp.1486–1489, May 2006</ref><ref>Wang, Z.H.; Javadi, H.H.S.; Epstein, A.J.; "Application of microwave cavity perturbation techniques in conducting polymers," Instrumentation and Measurement Technology Conference, 1991. IMTC-91. Conference Record., 8th IEEE, vol., no., pp.79–82, 14–16 May 1991</ref><ref>Ogunlade, O.; Yifan Chen; Kosmas, P.; "Measurement of the complex permittivity of microbubbles using a cavity perturbation technique for contrast enhanced ultra-wideband breast cancer detection," Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC), 2010 Annual International Conference of the IEEE, vol., no., pp.6733–6736, Aug. 31 2010-Sept. 4 2010</ref>

==Examples==

=== {{math|1=''TE''<sub>10''n''</sub>}} rectangular waveguide cavity ===

[[Image:Material cavity.JPG|thumb|center|upright=3|alt=A rectangular waveguide cavity with material sample.|Material sample introduced into rectangular waveguide cavity.]]

For rectangular waveguide cavity, field distribution of dominant [[Waveguide (electromagnetism)#Analysis|<math> TE_{10n} </math>]] mode is well known. Ideally, the material to be measured is introduced into the cavity at the position of maximum electric or magnetic field.  When the material is introduced at the position of maximum [[electric field]], then the contribution of magnetic field to perturbed frequency shift is very small and can be ignored. In this case, we can use perturbation theory to derive expressions for real and imaginary components of complex material permittivity <math>\epsilon_r = \epsilon_r'+j\epsilon_r''</math> as:<ref name=Mathew2005 />

{{NumBlk|:|<math>\epsilon_r'-1=\frac{f_c-f_s}{2f_s}\frac{V_c}{V_s}\,</math>|{{EquationRef|8}}}}

{{NumBlk|:|<math>\epsilon_r''=\frac{V_c}{4V_s}\frac{Q_c-Q_s}{Q_cQ_s}\,</math>|{{EquationRef|9}}}}

where <math>f_c</math> and <math>f_s</math> represent resonant frequencies of original cavity and perturbed cavity respectively, <math>V_c</math> and <math>V_s</math> represent volumes of original cavity and material sample respectively, <math>Q_c</math> and <math>Q_s</math> represent [[Q factor|quality factors]] of original and perturbed cavities respectively.

Once the complex permittivity of the material is known, we can easily calculate its effective [[Electrical resistivity and conductivity|conductivity]] <math> \sigma_e </math> and [[dielectric]] [[loss tangent]] <math>\tan\delta</math> as:<ref name=Mathew2005 />

{{NumBlk|:|<math>\sigma_e=\omega\epsilon''=2\pi f\epsilon_0\epsilon_r''\,</math>|{{EquationRef|10}}}}

{{NumBlk|:|<math>tan \delta=\frac{\epsilon_r''}{\epsilon_r'}\,</math>|{{EquationRef|11}}}}

where f is the frequency of interest and <math>\epsilon_0</math> is the free space permittivity.

Similarly, if the material is introduced into the cavity at the position of maximum magnetic field, then the contribution of electric field to perturbed frequency shift is very small and can be ignored. In this case, we can use perturbation theory to derive expressions for complex material permeability <math>\mu_r = \mu_r'+j\mu_r''</math> as:<ref name=Mathew2005 />
{{NumBlk|:|<math>\mu_r'-1=(\frac{\lambda_g^2+4a^2}{8a^2})(\frac{f_c-f_s}{f_s})(\frac{V_c}{V_s})\,</math>|{{EquationRef|12}}}}

{{NumBlk|:|<math>\mu_r''=(\frac{\lambda_g^2+4a^2}{16a^2})(\frac{V_c}{V_s})(\frac{Q_c-Q_s}{Q_cQ_s})\,</math>|{{EquationRef|13}}}}

where <math>\lambda_g</math> is the guide wavelength (calculated as <math>\lambda_g=\frac{2l}{n}</math>).
